procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but the case concerns selections made by the High Court of Kerala.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The challenge is to the selection process conducted by the High Court of Kerala in 2013 and 2014, specifically the introduction of minimum cut-off marks for the viva-voce (interview) *after* the selection process had already commenced, and the subsequent removal of candidates from the original merit list based on this new criterion.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Kerala conducted selections in 2013 and 2014 without initially setting cut-off marks for the viva-voce. After the interviews, an Administrative Committee (consisting of the same members as the Selection Committee) decided to impose minimum qualifying marks for the viva-voce, and a revised merit list was created based on this new criterion. This revised list was approved by the Full Court of the High Court, and appointments were made accordingly.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached because the petitioners challenged the High Court's selection process. The Supreme Court notes that a similar issue regarding changing selection criteria mid-process was raised in *Tej Prakash Pathak and others v. Rajesthan High Court and others*, where the correctness of the earlier decision in *Manjusree* was doubted, and the matter was referred to a larger bench. Another similar case, *Salam Samarjeet Singh v. High Court of Manipur At Imphal and Anr*, was also posted along with *Tej Prakash*. Given these circumstances, the Supreme Court decided to refer the present case (*Sivanandan C.T. & Ors. v. High Court of Kerala & Ors.*) to a larger bench to be heard along with *Tej Prakash*.

directions: Referring the matter to the larger Bench.

issue.issue_text: Whether the introduction of a minimum marks requirement for an interview after the selection process has commenced is impermissible on the ground that it amounts to changing the rules of the game after the game was played.

facts: A selection process for District & Sessions Judges was initiated, involving a written examination and a viva-voce (interview).
The initial rules stipulated minimum qualifying marks for the written exam to be eligible for the interview.

A prior Full Court Resolution from 2012 explicitly stated there should be no minimum cut-off marks for the interview, and the final merit list would be based on the total marks from both the written exam and the interview.
After the interviews were conducted, the Administrative Committee introduced a new rule requiring candidates to secure minimum marks in the interview as well.
This new requirement altered the final merit list and was challenged on the grounds that it amounted to changing the rules of the selection process after it had already commenced.
law: The Court identified the precedent set in *K. Manjusree v. State of Andhra Pradesh*, which held that introducing a minimum marks requirement for an interview after the selection process is complete is "clearly impermissible" as it amounts to "changing the rules of the game after the game was played."

The Court also noted a subsequent case, *Tej Prakash Pathak v. Rajesthan High Court*, which had specifically doubted the correctness of the *Manjusree* decision on this point and had referred the issue to a larger Bench for an authoritative ruling.
application: The Court found that the facts of the current case were "squarely" covered by the precedent in *K. Manjusree*. Based on this precedent alone, the introduction of minimum interview marks would be impermissible.
However, the Court could not definitively apply the *Manjusree* ruling because its correctness was already under review by a larger Bench due to the reference made in the *Tej Prakash* case.
Given that the core legal principle was unsettled and pending an authoritative pronouncement, the Court determined that it could not resolve the issue itself.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not provide a final decision on the issue. Recognizing that the precedent in *K. Manjusree* directly applied but its correctness had been doubted in *Tej Prakash Pathak*, the Court referred the matter to a larger Bench to be heard along with the other pending cases to settle the legal question authoritatively.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the introduction of a minimum marks requirement for an interview after the selection process has commenced is impermissible on the ground that it amounts to changing the rules of the game after the game was played.
appellant_arguments: The selection process was initiated based on a resolution that explicitly stated there would be no minimum cut-off marks for the interview.
The Administrative Committee introduced a minimum percentage of marks for the viva-voce only after the interviews were already conducted.
This act constitutes an impermissible change to the rules of the selection process after it had already started.
respondent_arguments: Fixing minimum marks for the viva-voce was not a deviation from the approved scheme.
It was always the intention of the Full Court to select only those candidates who meet a minimum required benchmark for such a responsible post.
Therefore, implementing a minimum mark requirement was a clarification of the existing standard, not a change in the rules.

cases.case_name: K. Manjusree v. State of Andhra Pradesh and another
cases.principle: The introduction of a requirement for minimum marks for an interview after the entire selection process is complete amounts to changing the rules of the game after the game was played, which is impermissible.

cases.case_name: Tej Prakash Pathak and others v. Rajasthan High Court and others
cases.principle: For doubting the correctness of the principle laid down in the K. Manjusree case and referring the issue to a larger bench for an authoritative pronouncement.

cases.case_name: Salam Samarjeet Singh v. High Court of Manipur At Imphal and Anr.
cases.principle: As a case dealing with a similar issue that has also been posted to be heard by a larger bench along with the Tej Prakash case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a legal issue is already pending before a larger bench for an authoritative pronouncement due to doubted precedents, it is appropriate to refer a similar matter to that larger bench for hearing.
obiter: Introduction of the requirement of minimum marks for an interview, after the entire selection process is completed, amounts to changing the rules of the game after the game was played, which is impermissible.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that while the precedent in K. Manjusree v. State of Andhra Pradesh, which held that introducing minimum interview marks after the selection process has started is impermissible, squarely applies to the facts of this case, the correctness of that very precedent has been specifically doubted and referred to a larger bench in the case of Tej Prakash Pathak and others v. Rajesthan High Court. Therefore, the court concluded that it is appropriate to refer the present matter to a larger bench as well, to be heard alongside the existing reference, for an authoritative pronouncement on the issue.
legal_tests_applied: The doctrine that "changing the rules of the game after the game was played... is clearly impermissible," as established in K. Manjusree v. State of Andhra Pradesh.

The principle of judicial propriety that when a precedent is under review by a larger bench due to doubts about its correctness (as seen in Tej Prakash Pathak's reference regarding Manjusree), similar subsequent cases should also be referred to that larger bench for a consistent and authoritative decision.
why_appellant_lost: The legal precedent they relied upon, K. Manjusree v. State of Andhra Pradesh, which held that changing selection rules mid-process is impermissible, has had its correctness specifically doubted by a subsequent bench in Tej Prakash Pathak and others v. Rajesthan High Court.

Because the core legal issue is already the subject of a reference to a larger bench for an authoritative pronouncement, this court cannot grant immediate relief and must also refer the matter for a consistent outcome.
why_respondent_won: The legal principle that would have definitively invalidated their action—the rule against changing selection criteria from K. Manjusree—is no longer considered settled law, as its correctness has been questioned and referred to a larger bench in the Tej Prakash Pathak case.
The existence of this doubt and the pending reference to a larger bench prevented the court from ruling against the respondent and instead necessitated a referral of the current case as well.
policy_considerations: The need for an authoritative pronouncement from a larger bench to settle the conflicting judicial views on whether it is permissible to change selection criteria after the process has commenced, ensuring consistency and clarity in the law.
